excerpt: The household and garage tools that send tens of thousands of people to the emergency room each year, and when a defective tool becomes a product liability claim.
keyTakeaways: Keep the tool that injured you, its packaging and any manual, and act quickly: Georgia generally allows two years to sue (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and bars strict liability claims more than ten years after a product's first sale (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11(b)(2)), while South Carolina allows three years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530(5)) with no repose period. Georgia holds the manufacturer strictly liable for a defective tool, but not a seller that did not make it (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11.1). South Carolina holds any seller of a defective, unreasonably dangerous product strictly liable, retailers included (S.C. Code § 15-73-10). CPSC estimates about 30,600 emergency-room table saw blade-contact injuries a year (2010-2021 data), 96.4 percent of them to the finger in its 2017 study. The CDC reports about 36,000 emergency-room visits a year for chainsaw injuries.

faqs.question: Which garage tool causes the most serious injuries?
faqs.answer: The table saw is arguably the most dangerous tool a person can own. Its high-speed rotating blade presents a risk of laceration and amputation, and CPSC estimates about 30,600 emergency-room blade-contact injuries a year (2010-2021 data); in 2017, about 2,800 of 26,500 were amputations.

faqs.question: What injuries do common power tools cause?
faqs.answer: Tool-related accidents can result in amputation, puncture wounds, brain injury, broken bones, burn injuries and even death. The severity is often out of proportion to how routine the task felt.

faqs.question: Why do safety mechanisms not prevent these injuries?
faqs.answer: Because most injuries are direct hand contact with the blade: in CPSC's 2017 study, 96.4 percent of table saw blade-contact injuries involved the finger, and CPSC found no downward trend from 2004 to 2021 despite blade guards and riving knives. That is why CPSC has proposed requiring blade-stopping technology.

faqs.question: Can I bring a claim if a defective tool injured me?
faqs.answer: You may be able to. Where a tool was defectively designed or manufactured, or lacked adequate warnings, a product liability claim can target the manufacturer: in Georgia the manufacturer is strictly liable (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11); in South Carolina any seller of a defective, unreasonably dangerous product is (S.C. Code § 15-73-10). Preserve the tool exactly as it is after the injury.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a product liability claim in Georgia or South Carolina?
faqs.answer: Georgia generally allows two years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33), but no strict liability action may be brought more than ten years after the product's first sale (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11(b)(2)), and that bar also covers negligence claims against the manufacturer, with narrow exceptions (O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11(c)). South Carolina allows three years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530(5)), running from when you knew or reasonably should have known of the claim (S.C. Code § 15-3-535), and has no statute of repose for product claims. Keeping the tool, its packaging and any manual is what makes such a claim provable.
